sources.fact: Cleveland Clinic, 'Earwax (Cerumen)': earwax isn't really wax; it is mostly sebum, dead skin cells and hair; made by sebaceous glands and ceruminous glands (modified sweat glands) in the ear canal; it traps dirt and dust and releases substances that protect against bacterial and fungal infections; ears are self-cleaning, chewing or talking gradually work the wax out; never stick cotton swabs into your ear

Cleveland Clinic Health Essentials (Jenaye Baker, PA-C): earwax has anti-fungal and anti-bacterial properties; ears naturally move wax outward; swab packages warn 'Do not insert swabs into the ear canal'; a swab pushes earwax deeper; get checked if your ear hurts, your hearing is muffled, you feel dizzy, or you have ringing

post.instagram_caption:
Earwax isn't wax 👂

It's mostly skin oil, dead skin cells and hair, made by glands in your ear canal, some of them modified sweat glands. It traps dirt and dust and helps fight bacteria and fungi. Your ears clean themselves: chewing and talking slowly move the wax out, like a tiny conveyor belt. Cotton swabs can push it deeper, and the box itself says not to put them in your ear. See a doctor if your ear hurts, your hearing goes muffled or you feel dizzy.

It's not wax. And it's not your job.

Sources: Cleveland Clinic, Hearing Health Foundation.
